n: Mormon picks up the story after the war of Alma 28. The converted Lamanites, the people of Ammon, are now settled safely in Jershon, and the invading Lamanites have been driven out and the dead buried.
The losses were so great no one counted the dead. After a season of fasting, mourning, and prayer, the sixteenth year of the judges (about 76 BC) brings a long-awaited peace.
The Nephites live the law of Moses faithfully, understanding that it pointed forward to Christ and would be kept only until He fulfilled it.
The entire sixteenth year passes without trouble—a rare and welcome stretch of calm in a war-filled record.
Peace continues into the seventeenth year of the judges.
Late that year a man arrives in Zarahemla preaching against prophecies of Christ. Mormon calls him an “Anti-Christ”: someone who opposes Christ and His saving role.
Nephite law protected freedom of belief. God Himself forbade laws that would treat people unequally because of what they believed.

f.w: no law against a man's belief

n: Mormon quotes Joshua’s famous challenge: each person must freely choose whom to serve. Real faith cannot be forced.

f.w: Choose ye this day, whom ye will serve

n: Worshipping God was a privilege for believers, but unbelief was not a crime. No one was punished simply for not believing.
Actions that hurt others were a different matter. Murder, robbery, theft, and adultery all carried penalties under the law.
The principle is summed up: people were judged for crimes they committed, not for beliefs they held. That fairness put everyone “on equal grounds.”
The man’s name is Korihor. Because he only preached ideas, the law could not touch him. His core message: there will be no Christ.
Korihor mocks believers as people chained to a silly hope. His argument: nobody can know the future, so looking for a coming Christ is foolish.

f.g: Harness yourselves like oxen—that is, burden yourselves.

n: He dismisses the prophets’ words as nothing more than inherited myths—“foolish traditions of your fathers.”
Korihor claims that only what you can see can be known. Alma will later answer that faith and evidence work differently than eyesight.

f.w: ye cannot know of things which ye do not see

n: He says the peace believers feel when their sins are forgiven is just a mental disorder caused by tradition—an attempt to explain away spiritual experience.

f.g: Forgiveness; the canceling of sin’s debt.

n: Korihor’s philosophy: no atonement, no sin, survival of the smartest and strongest. If nothing is a crime, then anything goes.

f.g: One’s own human effort and cleverness, without God.

n: His teachings bear their fruit: people throw off restraint and many fall into sexual sin, believing death is the end and there is no judgment.

f.w: when a man was dead, that was the end thereof

n: Korihor next tries his message in Jershon among the people of Ammon, the converted Lamanites who had buried their weapons.
These converts were wiser than many Nephites. They did not debate him; they brought him straight to Ammon, their high priest.
Ammon has him escorted out. In Gideon he gets nowhere too—he is bound and brought before the high priest and the chief judge of that land.
The high priest asks why Korihor twists the Lord’s ways and spoils people’s joy by telling them there is no Christ.

f.g: Twisting something good into something false.

n: The high priest is Giddonah. Korihor accuses religion of being a tool priests use to control people, keep them ignorant, and gain power.

f.g: To seize power one has no right to.

n: Korihor flips everything around: what believers call freedom he calls bondage, and he insists they cannot truly know their prophecies are true.

He attacks the idea that people suffer from the Fall of Adam. He says children are not guilty for a parent’s sin—a point the Book of Mormon itself agrees with in a different sense, since Christ’s atonement covers Adam’s transgression.

f.w: a child is not guilty because of its parents

n: He repeats that no one can know there will be a Christ, let alone one who will be killed for the world’s sins.

f.w: slain for the sins of the world

n: Korihor accuses the priests of keeping people down so they can live off others’ hard work, too afraid to enjoy their rights.

f.g: To stuff oneself; here, to live greedily off others.

n: He paints God as an imaginary being, invented through dreams and visions to frighten people into obeying priests. It is a complete denial of God’s existence.

f.g: Supposed secret knowledge that he claims is fake.

n: Seeing that Korihor will even speak against God, the leaders stop arguing. They send him under guard to Zarahemla to face Alma and the chief judge, Nephihah.
Before Alma and the chief judge, Korihor keeps right on blaspheming.

f.g: To speak with contempt about God or sacred things.

n: With grand, puffed-up language he accuses Alma and the church’s teachers of getting rich off the people.
Alma answers with plain facts: he has supported himself with his own hands for years while traveling to preach.

f.w: with mine own hands for my support

n: Neither Alma nor his fellow leaders have received a single coin for church work. Only judges were paid, and only a legal wage for their time.
So why would they do it, if not for money? Alma explains that their only reward is the joy of seeing others embrace the truth.
Alma presses Korihor: you know we get no gain. Do you really think we are deceiving people when it brings such joy into their hearts?
Korihor flatly answers yes. He insists the church’s joy is built on a lie, even with no evidence of anyone profiting from it.
Alma asks the central question directly: do you believe there is a God?
Korihor says no. Notice that by verse 52 he will admit he had always known there was a God.
Alma bears his own testimony: he knows there is a God and that Christ will come.

f.w: I know there is a God

n: Alma points out that Korihor has no actual evidence against God—only his own assertion.
By contrast, Alma says, everything around them testifies of God. He asks whether Korihor can honestly deny all of it.
Alma discerns that Korihor actually knows better. He has pushed away God’s Spirit and let the devil lead him around as a tool to destroy others.
Korihor demands a sign: show me God’s power, and then I will believe.

Alma replies that Korihor already has plenty of evidence: the testimony of believers and prophets, the scriptures, and the whole created order—the earth, its motion, and the planets moving in order all testify of a Creator.

f.w: all the planets which move in their regular form

f.g: To put God to the test, demanding proof.

n: Alma asks how Korihor can deny all these witnesses while leading people astray. Korihor doubles down: he will deny unless he is shown a sign.
Alma expresses real sorrow. He is grieved that Korihor keeps resisting the truth, putting his own soul in danger.
Still, it is better for one man to lose his soul than to drag many others down with him. Alma warns that if Korihor denies again, God will strike him unable to speak.

f.w: better that thy soul should be lost

n: Korihor shifts his wording—he doesn’t “deny” God but doesn’t “believe” in Him either—and again insists on a sign.
Alma gives the sign Korihor asked for: in God’s name, he will be struck dumb.
Instantly, Korihor loses the ability to speak, just as Alma said.
The chief judge writes to Korihor: are you convinced now? Would you have wanted someone else to suffer for your sign? You have your sign; will you keep arguing?
Korihor writes back an astonishing admission: only God’s power could do this—and he had always known there was a God.

He confesses the devil appeared to him as an angel and taught him what to say. His ideas spread because they appealed to people’s carnal desires, and their success eventually convinced even Korihor himself.

f.w: in the form of an angel

f.g: A mind focused on physical appetites and worldly desires.

n: Korihor begs Alma to pray that the curse be lifted.
Alma declines, knowing Korihor would return to deceiving people, and leaves the matter in the Lord’s hands.
The curse remains. Korihor is cast out and reduced to begging for food door to door.
The chief judge publishes what happened throughout the land and urges Korihor’s followers to repent quickly before similar judgments fall on them.
The people are convinced and return to the Lord, ending Korihor’s movement. Meanwhile Korihor continues begging to survive.
Wandering among the Zoramites, a group that had broken away from the Nephites under a man named Zoram, Korihor is run over and trampled to death.
Mormon draws the lesson: those who twist the Lord’s ways come to a bitter end, because the devil does not stand by his followers. He uses them and then drops them.

f.w: the devil will not support his children
